PETITION FOR CHANGE OF NAME (ADULT OR MINOR) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan A. Rivera · Jordan Alexander Rivera

DECLARATION OF PURPOSE — PETITION FOR CHANGE OF NAME INFORMATION SHEET
This Petition for Change of Name — Information Sheet concerns a proposed change from Jordan Alexander Rivera's present legal name to the proposed name Jordan Alexander Reyes. It is prepared for use alongside an actual petition for change of name that would be filed by Jordan A. Rivera in the California superior court for Sacramento County. This information sheet describes California's statutory change-of-name petition process — who may file, what the petition must state, the order to show cause and publication requirements, and the standard a court applies in deciding whether to grant or deny the petition — as background for that filing. It is not itself a court filing, and completing it does not change Jordan Alexander Rivera's legal name in any respect. Only a court order (a decree granting the petition) can actually change a person's legal name through this process.

WHERE AND HOW A CHANGE-OF-NAME PETITION IS FILED
California Code of Civil Procedure § 1275 provides that applications for change of names must be determined by the Superior Courts. Under § 1276(a)(1), an application for change of name is made to the superior court of the county where the person whose name is proposed to be changed resides, and is filed either by petition signed by that person or, if the person is under 18 years of age, by one of the person's parents, by any guardian of the person, or, if both parents are deceased and there is no guardian, by a near relative or friend of the person. Under § 1276(a)(2), the petition must specify the place of birth and residence of the person, the person's present name, the name proposed, and the reason for the change of name. A narrower, separately added venue rule in § 1276(g)(1) allows a person who does not reside in California to file in the county tied to a California birth certificate or California marriage license the person is seeking to change; that limited nonresident route is not the general filing rule this clause otherwise describes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Applications for change of names must be determined by the Superior Courts."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1275 (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 1275 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1275.)
  "All applications for change of names shall be made to the superior court of the county where the person whose name is proposed to be changed resides, except as specified in subdivision (e) or (g), either (A) by petition signed by the person or, if the person is under 18 years of age, by one of the person’s parents, by any guardian of the person, or as specified in subdivision (e), or, if both parents are deceased and there is no guardian of the person, then by some near relative or friend of the person, or (B) as provided in Section 7638 of the Family Code."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1276(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 1276(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1276.)
  "The petition or pleading shall specify the place of birth and residence of the person, the person’s present name, the name proposed, and the reason for the change of name."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1276(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 1276(a)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1276.)
  "On or after January 1, 2023, an application for a change of name may be made to a superior court for a person whose name is proposed to be changed, even if the person does not reside within the State of California, if the person is seeking to change their name on at least one of the following documents:"
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1276(g)(1) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 1276(g)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1276.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's name-change petition process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific name change. This document is informational: it does not itself change any person's legal name; only a court order (decree) granting the petition can do that. Three of these citations — § 1276(a)(1), § 1276(a)(2), and § 1276(g)(1) — are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1276); the fourth, § 1275, is a separate, one-sentence section establishing only that superior courts (rather than some other tribunal) decide these applications. This clause corrects an assumption in the original research brief, which asked to verify § 1277 as 'the actual statutory basis for filing a petition for change of name in superior court': on the verified statutory text, § 1276(a)(1) — not § 1277 — is the section that actually authorizes filing and states the superior-court, county-of-residence venue rule; § 1277 instead governs the order to show cause, hearing, and publication process that follows a filing, covered in this document's companion clauses. Section 1276(a)(1)(B)'s cross-reference to Family Code § 7638 — a name-change route available within a Uniform Parentage Act proceeding — is not detailed further here; that separate route is addressed by this corpus's Paternity Action (Petition to Establish Parental Relationship) Information Sheet document.

A MINOR'S NAME CHANGE: PETITION CONTENTS AND NOTICE TO THE OTHER PARENT
When the person whose name is proposed to be changed is under 18 years of age, several minor-specific requirements apply. Under § 1276(c), if a petition for a minor's name change is signed by only one parent, the petition must specify the other parent's address, if known and if that parent is living. Separately, under § 1277(a)(4), if a petition has been filed for a minor by one parent and the other parent, if living, does not join in consenting to it, the petitioner must cause notice of the hearing — or a copy of the order to show cause — to be served on the other parent at least 30 days before the hearing, in the manner used for service of a summons (or, where that cannot reasonably be accomplished, in a manner the court determines is reasonably calculated to give actual notice, which may include publication). Where a guardian, rather than a parent, files the petition on behalf of a minor ward, § 1277(f) separately requires the guardian to serve notice of the hearing on any living parent of the minor by personal service at least 30 days before the hearing, or, if a parent is deceased or cannot be located, to serve notice instead on the child's grandparents, if living.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In a proceeding for a change of name commenced by the filing of a petition, if the person whose name is proposed to be changed is under 18 years of age and the petition is signed by only one parent, the petition shall specify the address, if known, of the other parent if living."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1276(c) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 1276(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1276.)
  "If a petition has been filed for a minor by a parent and the other parent, if living, does not join in consenting thereto, the petitioner shall cause, not less than 30 days before the hearing, to be served notice of the time and place of the hearing or a copy of the order to show cause on the other parent pursuant to Section 413.10, 414.10, 415.10, or 415.40."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1277(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 1277(a)(4) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1277.)
  "If a guardian files a petition to change the name of the guardian’s minor ward pursuant to Section 1276: (1) The guardian shall provide notice of the hearing to any living parent of the minor by personal service at least 30 days before the hearing."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1277(f) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 1277(f) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1277.)

Two of these citations — § 1277(a)(4) and § 1277(f) — are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1277); § 1276(c) is a separate, independently cited section. This clause does not identify, and the statute does not itself provide, any minor-specific standard for resolving a notified parent's actual objection to a proposed name change of the parties' minor child: an objection instead triggers the same general objection-and-hearing process, and the same 'good cause' standard, described in this document's companion clause on the hearing standard, which applies without regard to whether the objecting party is a parent. Separately, § 1276(e) — not independently verified in full detail here — directs that petitions for a minor's name change filed by a guardian appointed by the juvenile or probate court, or by certain court-appointed attorneys for a minor in the juvenile-dependency or delinquency system, be made in the court already exercising jurisdiction over the minor, rather than under the general filing rule described in this document's companion clause; that narrower jurisdictional carve-out is not detailed further here.

THE ORDER TO SHOW CAUSE AND THE PUBLICATION REQUIREMENT
Once a petition for change of name is filed, § 1277(a)(1) requires the court to make an order reciting the filing of the petition and directing all interested persons to appear at a hearing set not less than 6 weeks nor more than 12 weeks from the date of the order (unless the court sets a different time), to show cause why the petition should not be granted; the order also directs that any written objection, stating the reasons for it, be filed with the court at least two court days before the hearing, and states that if no written objection is timely filed, the court may grant the petition without a hearing. Under § 1277(a)(2)(A), a copy of that order to show cause must be published, under Government Code § 6064, in a newspaper of general circulation designated in the order and published in the county (or, if none exists, posted by the clerk of the court in three of the most public places in the county). Under § 1277(a)(3), four weekly publications are sufficient to satisfy this requirement — specifically, publication once a week for four successive weeks is sufficient if the order is published in a daily newspaper.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The order shall direct all persons interested in the matter to appear before the court at a time and place specified, which shall be not less than 6 weeks nor more than 12 weeks from the time of making the order, unless the court orders a different time, to show cause why the application for change of name should not be granted. The order shall direct all persons interested in the matter to make known any objection that they may have to the granting of the petition for change of name by filing a written objection, which includes the reasons for the objection, with the court at least two court days before the matter is scheduled to be heard and by appearing in court at the hearing to show cause why the petition for change of name should not be granted. The order shall state that, if no written objection is timely filed, the court may grant the petition without a hearing."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1277(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 1277(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1277.)
  "A copy of the order to show cause shall be published pursuant to Section 6064 of the Government Code in a newspaper of general circulation to be designated in the order published in the county."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1277(a)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 1277(a)(2)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1277.)
  "Four weekly publications shall be sufficient publication of the order to show cause. If the order is published in a daily newspaper, publication once a week for four successive weeks shall be sufficient."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1277(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 1277(a)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1277.)

All three citations in this clause — § 1277(a)(1), § 1277(a)(2)(A), and § 1277(a)(3) — are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1277); no additional independent source was located or is cited for these requirements. THE CONFIDENTIAL AND SEALED-RECORD EXCEPTION TO PUBLICATION
California's name-change statute includes a distinct mechanism allowing certain petitioners to avoid the general publication requirement and to keep the current and proposed names confidential. Under § 1277(b)(1), if a petition alleges a reason described in paragraph (2) and the petitioner has established that the petitioner is an active participant in the state's address confidentiality program and that the name the petitioner is seeking to acquire is on file with the Secretary of State, the petition is exempt from the § 1277(a) publication requirement, and the petition and the court's order indicate only that the proposed name is confidential and on file with the Secretary of State, rather than reciting it. Under § 1277(b)(2), that procedure applies to petitions alleging any of four specific reasons: to avoid domestic violence, to avoid stalking, to avoid sexual assault, or to avoid human trafficking, each as defined by a cross-referenced statute. Under § 1277(b)(3), the petitioner's current legal name is likewise kept confidential by the court in that circumstance, and is not published or posted in the court's public calendars, indexes, or register of actions. Separately, under § 1277(b)(5), any petitioner may ask the court to file the petition and related papers under seal, which the court may grant only on findings that include that an overriding interest exists that overcomes the public's right of access to the record and that the interest supports sealing it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If the petition for a change of name alleges a reason or circumstance described in paragraph (2), and the petitioner has established that the petitioner is an active participant in the address confidentiality program created pursuant to Chapter 3.1 (commencing with Section 6205) of Division 7 of Title 1 of the Government Code, and that the name the petitioner is seeking to acquire is on file with the Secretary of State, the action for a change of name is exempt from the requirement for publication of the order to show cause under subdivision (a), and the petition and the order of the court shall, in lieu of reciting the proposed name, indicate that the proposed name is confidential and is on file with the Secretary of State pursuant to the provisions of the address confidentiality program."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1277(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 1277(b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1277.)
  "The procedure described in paragraph (1) applies to petitions alleging any of the following reasons or circumstances: (A) To avoid domestic violence, as defined in Section 6211 of the Family Code. (B) To avoid stalking, as defined in Section 646.9 of the Penal Code. (C) To avoid sexual assault, as defined in Section 1036.2 of the Evidence Code. (D) To avoid human trafficking, as defined in Section 236.1 of the Penal Code."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1277(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 1277(b)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1277.)
  "For any petition under this subdivision, the current legal name of the petitioner shall be kept confidential by the court and shall not be published or posted in the court’s calendars, indexes, or register of actions"
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1277(b)(3) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 1277(b)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1277.)
  "A petitioner may request that the court file the petition and any other papers associated with the proceeding under seal. The court may consider the request at the same time as the petition for name change, and may grant the request in any case in which the court finds that all of the following factors apply: (A) There exists an overriding interest that overcomes the right of public access to the record."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1277(b)(5) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 1277(b)(5) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1277.)

THE HEARING STANDARD AND THE COURT'S LIMITED GROUNDS TO DENY THE PETITION
If a written objection is timely filed, § 1278(a)(1) provides that the petition is heard only if the objection can show the court "good cause against the change of name"; at that hearing, the court may examine on oath any petitioner, objector, or other person concerning the petition, and may make an order granting the change of name or dismissing the petition, as the court deems right and proper. Under § 1278(a)(2), if no objection is filed at least two court days before the scheduled hearing, the court may grant the petition without a hearing. Where the confidentiality provisions of § 1277(b) apply, § 1278(b) separately requires that the court not disclose the proposed name unless the court finds, by clear and convincing evidence, that the petition's allegations of domestic violence, stalking, or sexual assault are false. Where a guardian, rather than a parent, files the petition on behalf of a minor ward, § 1278(d) requires the court first to find that the ward is likely to remain in the guardian's care until reaching the age of majority and is not likely to be returned to a parent's custody, and allows the court to grant the petition, upon making those findings, only if it also finds the proposed name change is in the child's best interest. Separately, under § 1279.5(e), a court must deny a name-change petition filed by a person required to register as a sex offender under Penal Code § 290, unless the court determines that granting it is in the best interest of justice and will not adversely affect public safety.

  "Except as provided in subdivisions (c) and (d), the petition or application shall be heard at the time designated by the court, only if objections are filed by a person who can, in those objections, show to the court good cause against the change of name. At the hearing, the court may examine on oath any of the petitioners, remonstrants, or other persons touching the petition or application, and may make an order changing the name, or dismissing the petition or application, as the court may deem right and proper."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1278(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 1278(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1278.)
  "If no objection is filed at least two court days before the date set for hearing, the court may, without hearing, enter the order that the change of name is granted."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1278(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 1278(a)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1278.)
  "If the provisions of subdivision (b) of Section 1277 apply, the court shall not disclose the proposed name unless the court finds by clear and convincing evidence that the allegations of domestic violence, stalking, or sexual assault in the petition are false."

  "If the petition for a change of name is filed by a guardian on behalf of a minor ward, the court shall first find that the ward is likely to remain in the guardian’s care until the age of majority and that the ward is not likely to be returned to the custody of the parents. Upon making those findings, the court shall consider the petition and may grant the petition only if it finds that the proposed name change is in the best interest of the child."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1278(d) (California Legislative Information text), CCP § 1278(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1278.)
  "Notwithstanding any other law, a court shall deny a petition for a name change pursuant to this title made by a person who is required to register as a sex offender under Section 290 of the Penal Code, unless the court determines that it is in the best interest of justice to grant the petition and that doing so will not adversely affect the public safety."

A NAME CHANGE TIED TO MARRIAGE OR DOMESTIC PARTNERSHIP USES A SEPARATE, NON-COURT PROCESS
A separate, simplified name-change mechanic exists for a name adopted in connection with marriage, and it does not involve filing a change-of-name petition under the court process described elsewhere in this document. Family Code § 306.5(a) provides that parties to a marriage are not required to have the same name, that neither party is required to change their name, and that a person's name does not change upon marriage unless that person elects to change it under subdivision (b). Under § 306.5(b)(1), a party may elect to change the middle or last name, or both, by which that party wishes to be known after the marriage, by entering the new name in the spaces provided on the marriage license application itself, without intent to defraud — a mechanism built into the marriage-license process rather than a separate court filing or hearing. A comparable no-court-petition mechanic applies to a name selected upon registration of a domestic partnership: Family Code § 298.5(e) provides that the Certificate of Registered Domestic Partnership issued by the Secretary of State includes both the name used by each party before registration and the new name, if any, selected by each party upon registration of the domestic partnership.

expectedJSON.body: California's name-change statute includes a distinct mechanism allowing certain petitioners to avoid the general publication requirement and to keep the current and proposed names confidential. Under § 1277(b)(1), if a petition alleges a reason described in paragraph (2) and the petitioner has established that the petitioner is an active participant in the state's address confidentiality program and that the name the petitioner is seeking to acquire is on file with the Secretary of State, the petition is exempt from the § 1277(a) publication requirement, and the petition and the court's order indicate only that the proposed name is confidential and on file with the Secretary of State, rather than reciting it. Under § 1277(b)(2), that procedure applies to petitions alleging any of four specific reasons: to avoid domestic violence, to avoid stalking, to avoid sexual assault, or to avoid human trafficking, each as defined by a cross-referenced statute. Under § 1277(b)(3), the petitioner's current legal name is likewise kept confidential by the court in that circumstance, and is not published or posted in the court's public calendars, indexes, or register of actions. Separately, under § 1277(b)(5), any petitioner may ask the court to file the petition and related papers under seal, which the court may grant only on findings that include that an overriding interest exists that overcomes the public's right of access to the record and that the interest supports sealing it.

expectedJSON.body: If a written objection is timely filed, § 1278(a)(1) provides that the petition is heard only if the objection can show the court "good cause against the change of name"; at that hearing, the court may examine on oath any petitioner, objector, or other person concerning the petition, and may make an order granting the change of name or dismissing the petition, as the court deems right and proper. Under § 1278(a)(2), if no objection is filed at least two court days before the scheduled hearing, the court may grant the petition without a hearing. Where the confidentiality provisions of § 1277(b) apply, § 1278(b) separately requires that the court not disclose the proposed name unless the court finds, by clear and convincing evidence, that the petition's allegations of domestic violence, stalking, or sexual assault are false. Where a guardian, rather than a parent, files the petition on behalf of a minor ward, § 1278(d) requires the court first to find that the ward is likely to remain in the guardian's care until reaching the age of majority and is not likely to be returned to a parent's custody, and allows the court to grant the petition, upon making those findings, only if it also finds the proposed name change is in the child's best interest. Separately, under § 1279.5(e), a court must deny a name-change petition filed by a person required to register as a sex offender under Penal Code § 290, unless the court determines that granting it is in the best interest of justice and will not adversely affect public safety.

expectedJSON.body: A separate, simplified name-change mechanic exists for a name adopted in connection with marriage, and it does not involve filing a change-of-name petition under the court process described elsewhere in this document. Family Code § 306.5(a) provides that parties to a marriage are not required to have the same name, that neither party is required to change their name, and that a person's name does not change upon marriage unless that person elects to change it under subdivision (b). Under § 306.5(b)(1), a party may elect to change the middle or last name, or both, by which that party wishes to be known after the marriage, by entering the new name in the spaces provided on the marriage license application itself, without intent to defraud — a mechanism built into the marriage-license process rather than a separate court filing or hearing. A comparable no-court-petition mechanic applies to a name selected upon registration of a domestic partnership: Family Code § 298.5(e) provides that the Certificate of Registered Domestic Partnership issued by the Secretary of State includes both the name used by each party before registration and the new name, if any, selected by each party upon registration of the domestic partnership.
